claims.text: Equimolar WTaTiVZr has greater plastic strain than commercially processed pure tungsten under high-temperature loading.
Equimolar WTaTiVZr has greater fracture toughness than commercially processed pure tungsten under high-temperature loading.
Equimolar mixing of W, Ta, Ti, V, and Zr produces local lattice distortions.
Compositional complexity creates heterogeneous internal stress fields.
Local lattice distortions lower the energy barrier for dislocation glide.
Lower glide barriers enhance dislocation mobility in WTaTiVZr.
Local lattice distortions promote faster dynamic recovery through dislocation annihilation or rearrangement.
Enhanced dislocation mobility and dynamic recovery reduce dislocation pile-ups and accumulated dislocation density.
Reduced dislocation pile-ups decrease stress concentrations that would otherwise cause premature failure.
Under identical loading, WTaTiVZr will exhibit faster dislocation motion than pure tungsten.
Under identical loading, WTaTiVZr will accumulate a lower dislocation density than pure tungsten.
Under identical loading, WTaTiVZr will have a higher dynamic-recovery rate than pure tungsten.
High-temperature, high-strain-rate testing near recrystallization mimics sustained plasma-facing-component service.
Matching grain size and texture between the alloy and pure tungsten makes intrinsic lattice heterogeneity the only variable.
Elemental segregation can influence deformation-related properties and therefore confound the proposed mechanism.
Prior related-RHEA evidence supports lattice-distortion-enhanced dislocation mobility.

contradictions.description: The conditions claim that lattice heterogeneity is the only variable, but replacing pure W with a five-element alloy simultaneously changes chemistry, bonding, elastic properties, diffusion, phase stability, and potentially defect energetics. Matching grain size and texture does not isolate lattice distortion as the sole causal variable.
